title: You read that story before. You almost skipped it.
paragraphs: You read that story before. You almost skipped it.
A borrowed axe head falls into the water… and then floats.
It sounded small. Strange. Easy to dismiss.
But here’s what most people don’t realize… that moment wasn’t about metal. It was about you.
Because you’ve lost things too.
Not just objects—weightier things. Conviction. Clarity. Fire. The sharp edge of your obedience. You didn’t mean to lose it. It slipped. One careless moment, one quiet compromise, one slow drift.
And then it was gone.
In 2 Kings, the sons of the prophets were working—building, expanding, moving forward. There was progress. Momentum. Purpose.
Until suddenly, a cry cut through the work:
“Alas, master! for it was borrowed.” (2 Kings 6:5)
Not owned. Borrowed.
That line should hit harder than it does.
Because the life you’re living… the breath in your lungs… the calling on your soul…
It was never yours to begin with.
God entrusted it to you.
And you knew.
You knew when your edge started dulling. You felt it when prayer became routine instead of desperation. When Scripture became optional instead of oxygen. When sin stopped shocking you.
God saw it.
The axe head didn’t drift away slowly. It sank instantly.
That’s how sin works.
One swing. One moment. One compromise.
And suddenly, what gave you effectiveness—your spiritual sharpness—is gone beneath the surface where you can’t reach it.
The man didn’t jump in after it.
He cried out.
That’s where everything changes.
Because most people don’t cry out anymore.
They adjust.
They pretend.
They keep swinging a stick, hoping no one notices the blade is gone.
But nothing is being cut.
Nothing is changing.
You can’t fake power.
When the man cried out, Elisha didn’t lecture him. He asked one question:
“Where did it fall?”
Location matters.
God doesn’t restore you in theory. He restores you at the point of loss.
That place you’ve been avoiding.
That conversation you keep postponing.
That sin you renamed so it feels smaller.
That’s where it fell.
And then something impossible happened.
Elisha cut a stick… threw it into the water… and the iron floated.
Iron doesn’t float.
Unless God intervenes.
Unless natural law bows to divine authority.
Unless grace steps into a place where effort has failed.
This wasn’t about physics.
It was about redemption.
Because everything in you that sank—every dull edge, every compromised moment, every hidden sin—cannot be retrieved by your own strength.
You cannot dive deep enough.
You cannot fix yourself.
But God can reverse what should stay lost.
And He doesn’t just point to it.
He makes it rise.
Now listen carefully.
The miracle didn’t end when the axe head floated.
Elisha said, “Take it up to yourself.”
The man had to reach.
Grace brought it back. Responsibility picked it up.
That’s where many stop.
They cry. They feel something. They get close again.
But they never reach.
They never repent.
And repentance is not emotion.
It’s turning.
It’s dropping the old patterns and actually picking up what God restored.
Now here’s where it goes deeper.
That floating iron is a shadow.
A preview.
Because centuries later, something heavier than iron sank into death.
Your sin.
Your guilt.
Your rebellion.
And unlike an axe head, it wasn’t an accident.
You chose it.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
Read that again.
All.
That includes the version of you that looks fine on the outside.
The one who smiles, scrolls, laughs—but knows there’s something missing underneath.
The weight is there.
And you can’t lift it.
But then came Jesus Christ.
Not with a stick thrown into water…
But with a cross planted into the earth.
“And God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
He stepped into the place where everything sank.
He took the weight.
And then He did what no one else could do—
He rose.
The resurrection is the ultimate “iron floating” moment.
What should stay buried… didn’t.
Death couldn’t hold Him.
Sin couldn’t define Him.
And if you’re in Him—it won’t define you either.
But here’s the tension you feel right now…
You know where it fell.
You know what you lost.
You know the exact moment your edge disappeared.
And now you’re standing at the water again.
Will you cry out?
Or will you keep pretending the blade is still there?
Because one path leads to quiet decay.
The other leads to confrontation… then restoration… then transformation.
Say it plainly—“I lost my edge.”
Not for attention.
For honesty.
And if you want to go deeper—real correction, real growth, real discipleship that sharpens you again—step into it here:
Because the difference between a dull life and a transformed one… is not effort.
It’s surrender to the One who makes dead things rise.
